Lecture 21

Quantum Calogero–Sutherland: integrability without a Bethe ansatz

What this lecture does

Every model since Lecture 15 has been solved by some form of Bethe ansatz. This lecture quantises Lecture 11’s Calogero–Moser gas and none of that machinery appears. The ground state is a product of powers, and one page of differentiation confirms it. The commuting charges come from operators that differentiate and permute at once — Dunkl operators — whose commutativity is a statement about transpositions, not about the Yang–Baxter equation. In a harmonic trap the whole spectrum is an arithmetic progression, the quantum face of Lecture 11’s isochrony. And what survives of the Bethe ansatz survives as a result, not a method.

21.1 The models, the units, and the domain

Lecture 11 studied NNN unit masses on a line with the pair potentials 1/x21/x^{2}1/x2, 1/sinh⁡2x1/\sinh^{2}x1/sinh2x, 1/sin⁡2x1/\sin^{2}x1/sin2x and ℘(x)\wp(x)℘(x) (Figure 21.1). Two of them are quantised here: the rational one in a harmonic trap, which is Lecture 11’s isochronous model (§11.6), and the trigonometric one, which is Sutherland’s.

This lecture uses ℏ=m=1\hbar=m=1ℏ=m=1, kinetic operator −12∑j∂j2-\tfrac12\sum_j\partial_j^{2}−21​∑j​∂j2​, so that Lecture 11’s H=12∑p2+g2∑VH=\tfrac12\sum p^{2}+g^{2}\sum VH=21​∑p2+g2∑V is its literal classical limit — and not the ℏ=2m=1\hbar=2m=1ℏ=2m=1 of Lecture 16, Lecture 19 and Lecture 20, which belongs to Lieb–Liniger. Why the coupling is written that way, and what the domain is

Near a collision the relative coordinate r=xi−xjr=x_i-x_jr=xi​−xj​ sees −∂r2+β(β−1)/r2-\partial_r^{2}+\beta(\beta-1)/r^{2}−∂r2​+β(β−1)/r2, whose solutions behave as rpr^{p}rp with p(p−1)=β(β−1)p(p-1)=\beta(\beta-1)p(p−1)=β(β−1): two exponents, p=βandp=1−β, p=\beta\quad\text{and}\quad p=1-\beta , p=βandp=1−β,(21.3) which the coupling does not distinguish checked. Fix β≥12\beta\ge\tfrac12β≥21​, choosing the larger — a labelling convention, not a stability condition, since β(β−1)=(β−12)2−14\beta(\beta-1)=(\beta-\tfrac12)^{2}-\tfrac14β(β−1)=(β−21​)2−41​ never falls below the Hardy bound −14-\tfrac14−41​, which it attains at β=12\beta=\tfrac12β=21​, where the exponents coincide and the second solution is r1/2ln⁡rr^{1/2}\ln rr1/2lnr.

Definition 21.2 (The model, completely). Take the ordered chamber — x1<⋯<xNx_1<\dots<x_Nx1​<⋯<xN​ on the line, and 0≤x1<⋯<xN<π0\le x_1<\dots<x_N<\pi0≤x1​<⋯<xN​<π on the circle, where xN−x1→πx_N-x_1\to\pixN​−x1​→π counts as a collision too — and define the operator as the Friedrichs extension of (21.1) or (21.2) from the smooth functions compactly supported away from every collision. On this domain an eigenfunction behaves at a collision as ψ=O(∣xi−xj∣β),xi→xj, \psi=O\bigl(\abs{x_i-x_j}^{\beta}\bigr),\qquad x_i\to x_j , ψ=O(∣xi​−xj​∣β),xi​→xj​,(21.4) the larger of the two exponents in (21.3). For β≥32\beta\ge\tfrac32β≥23​ the Friedrichs extension is the only self-adjoint one, the other branch r1−βr^{1-\beta}r1−β being not even locally square-integrable; for 12≤β<32\tfrac12\le\beta<\tfrac3221​≤β<23​ the operator is not essentially self-adjoint, and (21.4) is what picks this extension out of the family cited: Reed and Simon II, §X.1 and its appendix. For (21.2) there is a second, global condition: the model is bosonic and periodic, so a state extends from the chamber to a symmetric function of period π\piπ in each coordinate.

Two conventions follow and are used throughout. Restricting to the chamber and extending bosonically to RN\R^{N}RN are unitarily equivalent up to N!\sqrt{N!}N!​, so a symmetric function on RN\R^{N}RN and a function on the chamber are the same object; and Δ=∏i<j(xj−xi)\Delta=\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)Δ=∏i<j​(xj​−xi​) is positive there, so the symmetric function Δβ\Delta^{\beta}Δβ names is ∣Δ∣β\abs\Delta^{\beta}∣Δ∣β. And (21.4) describes eigenfunctions, not the whole operator domain, which contains functions with no pure power behaviour at all.

Example 21.3 (β=1\beta=1β=1: hard-core bosons, and free fermions). At β=1\beta=1β=1 the coupling vanishes but the boundary condition does not: it becomes ψ=0\psi=0ψ=0 at every collision. The particles are free and impenetrable — the Tonks–Girardeau gas of Proposition 19.7, here on a circle rather than on Lecture 14’s lattice. Girardeau’s map ψB=∏i<jsgn⁡(xi−xj) ψF\psi_{\mathrm B}=\prod_{i<j}\sgn(x_i-x_j)\,\psi_{\mathrm F}ψB​=∏i<j​sgn(xi​−xj​)ψF​ turns a fermionic state into a bosonic one at the same energy, and carrying one particle once round the circle multiplies the sign factor by (−1)N−1(-1)^{N-1}(−1)N−1 checked. So the impenetrable Bose gas on a ring is free fermions with antiperiodic boundary conditions when NNN is even and periodic ones when NNN is odd, as Lecture 19 said for the continuum gas cited: Girardeau (1960). For N=2N=2N=2 the allowed momenta on a circle of circumference π\piπ are then the odd integers, the two lowest are ±1\pm1±1, and E0=1E_0=1E0​=1. Theorem 21.13 will return that number from a formula that never mentions fermions.

Why it is the ground state, and why positivity is not the reason

The usual argument is that a positive eigenfunction of a Schrödinger operator on a connected domain is the ground state. That is true, and here it needs a hypothesis that is easy to drop.

Remark 21.5 (The partner exponent). Replacing β\betaβ by 1−β1-\beta1−β in ψ0S\psi_0^{\mathrm S}ψ0S​ changes neither (21.2) nor the positivity of the function on the chamber, and Theorem 21.4’s computation — which used only the exponent — makes it solve the same differential equation with the value (1−β)2N(N2−1)/6(1-\beta)^{2}N(N^{2}-1)/6(1−β)2N(N2−1)/6, strictly smaller than E0SE_0^{\mathrm S}E0S​ for β>12\beta>\tfrac12β>21​ checked. So positivity alone cannot identify the ground state. What excludes the partner is Definition 21.2, and the test is sharper than it looks: at N=2N=2N=2 the partner leaves L2L^{2}L2 exactly at β=32\beta=\tfrac32β=23​, but for N≥3N\ge3N≥3 the binding collision is the total one, where Δ1−β\Delta^{1-\beta}Δ1−β is homogeneous of degree (1−β)N(N−1)/2(1-\beta)N(N-1)/2(1−β)N(N−1)/2 in N−1N-1N−1 relative coordinates and its square is integrable only for β<1+1/N\beta<1+1/Nβ<1+1/N. A cluster of mmm particles gives β<1+1/m\beta<1+1/mβ<1+1/m, and 1+1/m1+1/m1+1/m decreases in mmm, so the total collision is the sharpest of the N−1N-1N−1 tests. At N=3N=3N=3, β=75\beta=\tfrac75β=57​ every pair test passes and the triple collision diverges checked. So the honest statement is that (21.5) is positive, lies in the form domain of Definition 21.2, and is the ground state of that operator sketched.

21.3 Dunkl operators

Lecture 11 got the classical charges from a Lax matrix; Lecture 17 got them from a transfer matrix. Neither route is taken here. Instead there is a family of first-order operators that commute outright — and they do it by carrying a transposition inside them.

Definition 21.6 (Dunkl operators). Let sijs_{ij}sij​ be the operator that exchanges the arguments xix_ixi​ and xjx_jxj​ of a function, (sijf)(…,xi,…,xj,… )=f(…,xj,…,xi,… )(s_{ij}f)(\dots,x_i,\dots,x_j,\dots)=f(\dots,x_j,\dots,x_i,\dots)(sij​f)(…,xi​,…,xj​,…)=f(…,xj​,…,xi​,…). For i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,Ni=1,…,N put Di=∂i+β∑j≠i1−sijxi−xj. D_i=\partial_i+\beta\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{1-s_{ij}}{x_i-x_j} . Di​=∂i​+βj=i∑​xi​−xj​1−sij​​.(21.7)

First, DiD_iDi​ maps polynomials to polynomials: (1−sij)f(1-s_{ij})f(1−sij​)f vanishes on xi=xjx_i=x_jxi​=xj​ and is therefore divisible by xi−xjx_i-x_jxi​−xj​, so no pole survives. That is a complete construction of a commuting family — infinitely many operators, NNN of them algebraically independent (the reading) — with no RRR-matrix, no transfer matrix and no ansatz. Of §13.5’s three criteria this lecture therefore uses neither (T) nor (P) — the trapped spectrum below is as far from Poisson as a spectrum gets — but supplies the charges directly, as Lecture 14 did, and meets (S) in the asymptotic sense of §21.6.

The operator on the right is triangular in the degree: ∑xi∂i\sum x_i\partial_i∑xi​∂i​ multiplies a homogeneous polynomial of degree ddd by ddd, and −12∑Di2-\tfrac12\sum D_i^{2}−21​∑Di2​ sends degree ddd into degree d−2d-2d−2 (Theorem 21.9), possibly to zero. Dyson’s three ensembles

Remark 21.16 (The ground state is a random-matrix ensemble). In the variable (21.15), ∣ψ0S∣2∝∏i<j∣zi−zj∣2β\abs{\psi_0^{\mathrm S}}^{2}\propto\prod_{i<j}\abs{z_i-z_j}^{2\beta}​ψ0S​​2∝∏i<j​∣zi​−zj​∣2β on the unit circle, which up to normalisation is the joint eigenvalue density of Dyson’s circular ensemble of index 2β2\beta2β cited: Dyson (1962); Mehta ch. 11. The three classical values β=12,1,2\beta=\tfrac12,1,2β=21​,1,2 are the orthogonal, unitary and symplectic ensembles, Dyson’s 1,2,41,2,41,2,4 — the three Wigner–Dyson curves Figure 13.4 drew for level statistics, appearing here as the positions of particles in a ground state (Figure 21.6). The repulsion exponent is the Jastrow exponent: P(s)∼s2βP(s)\sim s^{2\beta}P(s)∼s2β as s→0s\to0s→0 is the vanishing of ψ0S\psi_0^{\mathrm S}ψ0S​ at a collision, squared.

21.6 The dictionary: what is shared, and what is not

Nothing in this lecture was an RRR-matrix: no auxiliary space, no monodromy matrix, no RTTRTTRTT relation, and Corollary 21.10 is not { dkln⁡t(λ) }\{\,\dd^{k}\ln t(\lambda)\,\}{dklnt(λ)} for any ttt — Lecture 17’s tower comes from one transfer matrix and one solution of the Yang–Baxter equation, while IkI_kIk​ comes from NNN operators that commute before anything is traced. Nor was there a Bethe ansatz: Proposition 21.15 reports the answer in Bethe form rather than obtaining it. Both are claims about the route; the trigonometric model does carry a braid-group structure, Cherednik’s, and the reading says where.

What is shared: infinitely many commuting charges, one of them the Hamiltonian; a many-body problem fixed by two-body data, one exponent β\betaβ per pair, with free particles at shifted momenta; and non-diffractive scattering — criterion (S) of §13.5 — in the strongest form there is, the phase shift being constant. The difference is where the structure sits: in Lecture 17 and Lecture 18 in an algebra of operators on an auxiliary space, here in the symmetric group.

Dictionary

The classical Calogero–Moser gas obtained in Lecture 12 by reducing free motion on Hermitian matrices, the positions being the eigenvalues of a matrix moving freely⟶at β=1\beta=1β=1 the Sutherland model is free fermions, and in its ground state the e2ixje^{2\ii x_j}e2ixj​ are distributed exactly as the eigenvalues of a Haar-random unitary matrix (Remark 21.16) (type A)

Isochrony of the trapped model (Equation (11.10), Corollary 12.13): every orbit closes after 2π/ν2\pi/\freq2π/ν, whatever its energy⟶the equally spaced spectrum E0+νnE_0+\freq nE0​+νn (Theorem 21.11): every state returns after 2π/ν2\pi/\freq2π/ν, whatever its energy (type A)

21.7 Creation operators, Cherednik’s operators, and exclusion statistics

Four continuations, each of which is a small subject.

What the charges are, and what they are not. IkI_kIk​ of Corollary 21.10 is a differential–difference operator of order kkk involving every particle; it is not a sum of local densities of bounded range, and there is no lattice here for Definition 13.2 to apply to. The family is also not the one Lecture 11 produced classically: tr⁡Lk\tr L^{k}trLk quantises to something with ordering ambiguities, and the Dunkl construction sidesteps that question rather than answering it. What is true is that the IkI_kIk​ commute, that I2I_2I2​ is the Hamiltonian, and that NNN of them are algebraically independent — which is the count Liouville would have asked for cited: Polychronakos (1992).

Creation operators. Theorem 21.11 gives the trapped spectrum but not a ladder: it produces eigenvalues by triangularity, not by raising a state. A ladder exists, and it lives in the gauge-transformed picture, which is the thing to get right. Put ai±=12ν(νxi∓Di),[ai−,aj+]=[Di,xj]a_i^{\pm}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\freq}}\bigl(\freq x_i\mp D_i\bigr) , \qquad \comm{a_i^{-}}{a_j^{+}}=\comm{D_i}{x_j}ai±​=2ν​1​(νxi​∓Di​),[ai−​,aj+​]=[Di​,xj​] with (21.9) on the right: a deformed Heisenberg algebra whose deformation is made of transpositions. The symmetric combinations Bk+=∑i(ai+)kB_k^{+}=\sum_i(a_i^{+})^{k}Bk+​=∑i​(ai+​)k raise the energy by kνk\freqkν, and the NNN of them with k=1,…,Nk=1,\dots,Nk=1,…,N generate the whole spectrum freely — but from the Gaussian G=e−ν∑jxj2/2G=e^{-\freq\sum_jx_j^{2}/2}G=e−ν∑j​xj2​/2, not from ψ0C\psi_0^{\mathrm C}ψ0C​. The physical states are ΔβBk1+⋯Bkr+G\Delta^{\beta}B^{+}_{k_1}\cdots B^{+}_{k_r}GΔβBk1​+​⋯Bkr​+​G; equivalently, the physical ladders are Bk+=ΔβBk+Δ−β\mathcal B^{+}_k=\Delta^{\beta}B^{+}_k\Delta^{-\beta}Bk+​=ΔβBk+​Δ−β, applied to ψ0C\psi_0^{\mathrm C}ψ0C​ cited: Brink, Hansson and Vasiliev (1992), eqs. (2), (4), (12); Polychronakos (1992). Applying the displayed Bk+B_k^{+}Bk+​ to ψ0C\psi_0^{\mathrm C}ψ0C​ itself leaves the Hilbert space: at N=2N=2N=2, β=ν=1\beta=\freq=1β=ν=1, B2+ψ0CB_2^{+}\psi_0^{\mathrm C}B2+​ψ0C​ acquires a 2/r22/r^{2}2/r2 and is not square-integrable. With the gauge right, the spectrum is that of NNN independent bosonic modes of frequencies ν,2ν,…,Nν\freq,2\freq,\dots,N\freqν,2ν,…,Nν, so the multiplicity of E0+νnE_0+\freq nE0​+νn is the number of partitions of nnn into parts of size at most NNN — the conjugate of Theorem 21.11’s count, and equal to it. That is also why the multiplicities do not depend on β\betaβ.

Cherednik’s operators. The DiD_iDi​ of (21.7) are the rational Dunkl operators, and Theorem 21.13 did not use them: the Sutherland model needed its own conjugation, done by hand. There is a trigonometric analogue, Cherednik’s: commuting first-order differential–difference operators in zzz, built from zj∂zjz_j\partial_{z_j}zj​∂zj​​ and the transpositions, whose algebra is the degenerate affine Hecke algebra — and that is where the braid relations hidden in this model live. Two distinctions are easy to lose. The individual Cherednik operators do not preserve the symmetric polynomials; their eigenfunctions are the non-symmetric Jack polynomials, and it is their symmetric combinations that act on Λsym\Lambda^{\mathrm{sym}}Λsym and are diagonalised by the JκJ_\kappaJκ​ of Theorem 21.13. And the qqq-difference theory, where zj↦qzjz_j\mapsto qz_jzj​↦qzj​, is a different and larger story: it produces Macdonald polynomials and the double affine Hecke algebra, with the Jack polynomials recovered in a degeneration cited: Cherednik (1991); Macdonald §VI.10.

A discrepancy in the standard reference. Sutherland’s Beautiful Models §5.2.5 gives the trigonometric spectrum twice. Its first form, E=(2π2/L2)[∑jnj2+λ∑j>i∣nj−ni∣]+E0E=(2\pi^{2}/L^{2})\bigl[\sum_jn_j^{2} +\lambda\sum_{j>i}\abs{n_j-n_i}\bigr]+E_0E=(2π2/L2)[∑j​nj2​+λ∑j>i​∣nj​−ni​∣]+E0​ on a circle of circumference LLL, is (21.16) exactly, with λ=β\lambda=\betaλ=β, n=κn=\kappan=κ, L=πL=\piL=π. The last line of the same equation, and the momenta of §5.2.6, print kj=(2π/L)[nj+λ(N+1−2j)]k_j=(2\pi/L)[n_j+\lambda(N+1-2j)]kj​=(2π/L)[nj​+λ(N+1−2j)] — twice the shift, and inconsistent with the same book’s own E0=π2λ2N(N2−1)/6L2E_0=\pi^{2}\lambda^{2}N(N^{2}-1)/6L^{2}E0​=π2λ2N(N2−1)/6L2. The free-fermion case settles it: at λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, N=2N=2N=2, L=πL=\piL=π the ground state is sin⁡(x1−x2)\sin(x_1-x_2)sin(x1​−x2​), whose momenta are ±1\pm1±1 and whose energy is 111, which is that E0E_0E0​; the printed momenta give ±2\pm2±2 and 444. Replacing λ\lambdaλ by λ/2\lambda/2λ/2 in those two places repairs both checked; pages rendered, not extracted.

Fractional exclusion statistics. The density equation after Proposition 21.15 reads ρt=12π−(β−1)ρ\rho_t=\tfrac1{2\pi}-(\beta-1)\rhoρt​=2π1​−(β−1)ρ: each root present removes β−1\beta-1β−1 vacancies beyond the one it occupies. Haldane read this as a statistics interpolating between bosons and fermions, with β=1\beta=1β=1 the fermionic point where nothing is removed. The thermodynamics is then a one-line modification of Lecture 20’s counting — the binomial coefficient (LρtdλLρdλ)\binom{L\rho_t\dd\lambda}{L\rho\dd\lambda}(LρdλLρt​dλ​) of Proposition 20.1 acquires a β\betaβ-dependent number of slots — and reproduces the Calogero–Sutherland free energy cited: Haldane (1991); Wu (1994). It is the course’s cleanest example of a delta-function kernel: Lecture 19’s integral equation becomes local in momentum, and the thermodynamics is algebra rather than an integral equation.

21.8 Two particles, done by hand

Everything in this lecture is visible at N=2N=2N=2, where no symmetric-function theory is needed. Separate the centre of mass R=(x1+x2)/2R=(x_1+x_2)/2R=(x1​+x2​)/2 and the relative coordinate r=x2−x1>0r=x_2-x_1>0r=x2​−x1​>0 on the chamber. Five things to check, in this order.

(a) The ground state and the spectrum. The product of the two ground states is rβe−ν(2R2+r2/2)/2r^{\beta}e^{-\freq(2R^{2}+r^{2}/2)/2}rβe−ν(2R2+r2/2)/2, which is (21.5) at N=2N=2N=2, with E0=ν(12+β+12)=ν(1+β)E_0=\freq(\tfrac12+\beta+\tfrac12)=\freq(1+\beta)E0​=ν(21​+β+21​)=ν(1+β), matching (21.6). The full spectrum is E0+ν(ncm+2n)E_0+\freq(n_{\mathrm{cm}}+2n)E0​+ν(ncm​+2n), and the number of ways to write kkk as ncm+2nn_{\mathrm{cm}}+2nncm​+2n is ⌊k/2⌋+1\lfloor k/2\rfloor+1⌊k/2⌋+1, the partitions of kkk into at most two parts. Theorem 21.11 at N=2N=2N=2, obtained without a single Dunkl operator — and, unlike the theorem, with completeness thrown in, since the radial problem’s eigenfunctions are a known complete set. A finite-difference diagonalisation of hrelh_{\mathrm{rel}}hrel​ confirms the levels and finds nothing between them.

(b) The domain is doing work. The other indicial root gives r1−βe−νr2/4r^{1-\beta}e^{-\freq r^{2}/4}r1−βe−νr2/4, also positive, also a solution, with the lower value ν(32−β)\freq(\tfrac32-\beta)ν(23​−β). At the endpoint β=12\beta=\tfrac12β=21​ the two exponents coincide, the second solution is r1/2ln⁡rr^{1/2}\ln rr1/2lnr, and the two values are equal: there is nothing to choose between. (d) Bohr–Sommerfeld, exactly. For A>0A>0A>0 and E>νAE>\freq\sqrt AE>νA​ the classical orbit of hrelh_{\mathrm{rel}}hrel​ with coupling AAA has two turning points and action ∮p dr/2π=(E/ν−A)/2\oint p\,\dd r/2\pi=(E/\freq-\sqrt A)/2∮pdr/2π=(E/ν−A​)/2, so I=n+12I=n+\tfrac12I=n+21​ gives E=ν(2n+1+A)E=\freq(2n+1+\sqrt A)E=ν(2n+1+A​). That is the exact level ν(2n+β+12)\freq(2n+\beta+\tfrac12)ν(2n+β+21​) if and only if A=β−12\sqrt A=\beta-\tfrac12A​=β−21​: the Langer value A=(β−12)2A=(\beta-\tfrac12)^{2}A=(β−21​)2, not the bare A=β(β−1)A=\beta(\beta-1)A=β(β−1). On the circle, ψ0S=sin⁡βr\psi_0^{\mathrm S}=\sin^{\beta}rψ0S​=sinβr and E0S=β2⋅2⋅3/6=β2E_0^{\mathrm S}=\beta^{2}\cdot2\cdot3/6=\beta^{2}E0S​=β2⋅2⋅3/6=β2; and (21.16) gives k1,2=2κ1,2±βk_{1,2}=2\kappa_{1,2}\pm\betak1,2​=2κ1,2​±β, so Eκ=12[(2κ1+β)2+(2κ2−β)2]E_\kappa=\tfrac12\bigl[(2\kappa_1+\beta)^{2}+(2\kappa_2-\beta)^{2}\bigr]Eκ​=21​[(2κ1​+β)2+(2κ2​−β)2]. The formal value β=0\beta=0β=0 gives free bosons at rest, E=0E=0E=0 — the one exponent at which the shift disappears, and the only one at which the ground state is not an ensemble. It lies outside Definition 21.2’s β≥12\beta\ge\tfrac12β≥21​, being the partner of β=1\beta=1β=1.

Summary

  • The models (21.1), (21.2), in units ℏ=m=1\hbar=m=1ℏ=m=1 (Remark 21.1) with coupling β(β−1)\beta(\beta-1)β(β−1); the operator is the Friedrichs extension and its eigenfunctions vanish as ∣xi−xj∣β\abs{x_i-x_j}^{\beta}∣xi​−xj​∣β (Definition 21.2) — the larger indicial exponent, and a genuine part of the model.
  • Jastrow ground states (Theorem 21.4): E0=ν(N/2+βN(N−1)/2)E_0=\freq(N/2+\beta N(N-1)/2)E0​=ν(N/2+βN(N−1)/2) trapped, E0=β2N(N2−1)/6E_0=\beta^{2}N(N^{2}-1)/6E0​=β2N(N2−1)/6 on the circle, both by one page of differentiation. Positivity is not what makes them ground states (Remark 21.5): for β>12\beta>\tfrac12β>21​ the partner function ∏sin⁡1−β\prod\sin^{1-\beta}∏sin1−β is positive too and solves the same equation with a lower value, and the form domain is what excludes it — for N≥3N\ge3N≥3 by the total collision, β<1+1/N\beta<1+1/Nβ<1+1/N, not by any pair. At β=12\beta=\tfrac12β=21​ the two coincide.
  • Dunkl operators (21.7) commute (Theorem 21.8; the N=2N=2N=2 case is the translation invariance of x1−x2x_1-x_2x1​−x2​, and the general case follows in five lines from the commutator of DiD_iDi​ with a coordinate, in the reading), and on symmetric functions −12∑Di2-\tfrac12\sum D_i^{2}−21​∑Di2​ is the gauge-transformed Calogero operator (Theorem 21.9). Hence commuting charges Ik=∑DikI_k=\sum D_i^{k}Ik​=∑Dik​ with no transfer matrix and no ansatz (Corollary 21.10).
  • The trapped spectrum (21.14) is E0+νnE_0+\freq nE0​+νn with multiplicity p(n∣at most N parts)p(n\mid\text{at most }N\text{ parts})p(n∣at most N parts), by triangularity in the degree (Theorem 21.11) — and Dunkl commutativity is not needed for it. Its classical face is Lecture 11’s isochrony (Remark 21.12); Bohr–Sommerfeld reproduces it exactly once the coupling carries its Langer value (β−12)2(\beta-\tfrac12)^{2}(β−21​)2, and comparing that with the bare β(β−1)\beta(\beta-1)β(β−1) needs β>1\beta>1β>1.
  • Sutherland’s spectrum (21.16): E=12∑kj2E=\tfrac12\sum k_j^{2}E=21​∑kj2​ with kj=2κj+β(N+1−2j)k_j=2\kappa_j+\beta(N+1-2j)kj​=2κj​+β(N+1−2j) on the circle of circumference π\piπ — free fermions with momenta spread by 2β2\beta2β per pair, eigenfunctions the Jack polynomials (Theorem 21.13), whose triangularity argument needs dominance monotonicity, not distinctness. Those kjk_jkj​ solve Lecture 19’s unified Bethe equation (21.17) in the ordered sector, with the step φ=−π(β−1)sgn⁡k\varphi=-\pi(\beta-1)\sgn kφ=−π(β−1)sgnk and Lecture 16’s quantum numbers (Proposition 21.15) — and the β−1\beta-1β−1, not β\betaβ, is fixed by the density equation, not by the spectrum. The ansatz is a result here, not a method. The standard reference prints the shift twice as large; the reading records where.
  • Dyson (Remark 21.16): ∣ψ0S∣2\abs{\psi_0^{\mathrm S}}^{2}​ψ0S​​2 is the circular ensemble of index 2β2\beta2β, so β=12,1,2\beta=\tfrac12,1,2β=21​,1,2 are Dyson’s 1,2,41,2,41,2,4 — Lecture 13’s three curves, as a ground state.
